title: The Song of the Free
subject: English
chapter: 17. Poem: The Song of the Free
description: Grammar-focused practice for the chapter: punctuation (full stop, question mark, exclamation mark, comma, quotation marks, apostrophe for contractions and possession) and capitalization, with poem comprehension, vocabulary, and facts about the poet Swami Vivekananda from 'The Song of the Free'.

questions.question: What is a full stop used for?
options: To mark the end of a complete statement or command
questions.explanation: A full stop (.) signals the end of a complete statement or command.

questions.question: Which sentence ends with the correct punctuation mark?
questions.explanation: A statement ends with a full stop, so 'She walked out quietly.' is correct.

questions.question: A full stop is like a red traffic light that tells the reader to stop.
questions.explanation: The book compares a full stop to a red traffic light — it tells the reader to stop at the end of a complete thought.

questions.question: Which of these needs a full stop at the end?
questions.explanation: 'She picked up her bag' is a statement, so it needs a full stop. The others are questions or exclamations.

questions.question: How many full stops are needed here: 'She picked up her bag She walked out quietly'?
questions.explanation: There are two complete statements, so two full stops are needed: 'She picked up her bag. She walked out quietly.'

questions.question: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
options: The sun set. The stars came out.
The sun set the stars came out.
The sun set? The stars came out?
The sun set the stars came out!
questions.explanation: Two separate statements each need a full stop: 'The sun set. The stars came out.'

questions.question: A full stop is used at the end of a command like 'Close the door.'
questions.explanation: A full stop marks the end of a complete statement OR a command, such as 'Close the door.'

questions.question: Which sentence has a full stop used INCORRECTLY?
questions.explanation: 'Where. are you going' wrongly places a full stop in the middle. It should be a question: 'Where are you going?'

questions.question: A full stop shows that a thought is ____.
questions.explanation: A full stop shows that a complete thought or statement has ended.

questions.question: Which is the correct end mark for 'Please sit down'?
questions.explanation: 'Please sit down' is a polite command (a statement), so it ends with a full stop.

questions.question: Every complete sentence that is a plain statement should end with a full stop.
questions.explanation: Plain statements end with a full stop to show the thought is complete.

questions.question: Which correctly separates these two statements: 'I like tea I do not like coffee'?
options: I like tea. I do not like coffee.
I like tea I do not like coffee.
I like tea, I do not like coffee
I like tea? I do not like coffee?
questions.explanation: Two separate statements each need their own full stop.

questions.question: What symbol is a full stop?
questions.explanation: A full stop is written as a small dot (.).

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a full stop?
questions.explanation: A statement must end with a full stop: 'The dog barked loudly.'

questions.question: A full stop can be used at the end of a question.
questions.explanation: A question ends with a question mark (?), not a full stop. Full stops end statements and commands.

questions.question: Choose the sentence with correct end punctuation for a statement.
questions.explanation: This is a statement of fact, so it ends with a full stop.

questions.question: When do we use a question mark?
options: At the end of a sentence that asks something
At the end of a statement
questions.explanation: A question mark (?) is used at the end of a sentence that asks something.

questions.question: Which sentence needs a question mark?
options: Where did you put my notebook
questions.explanation: 'Where did you put my notebook' asks something, so it needs a question mark.

questions.question: A question mark signals that an answer is expected.
questions.explanation: A question mark shows that a question has been asked and an answer is expected.

questions.question: What symbol is a question mark?
questions.explanation: A question mark is written as (?).

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.explanation: 'What time is it' is a question, so it ends with a question mark: 'What time is it?'

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences that should end with a question mark.
questions.explanation: 'How are you' and 'Are you coming' ask questions. The other two are a statement and a command.

questions.question: Which words often begin a question?
options: Who, what, where, when, why, how
questions.explanation: Question words like who, what, where, when, why, and how usually begin questions.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a question mark INCORRECTLY?
questions.explanation: 'I like ice cream' is a statement, so it should end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: The sentence 'Are you ready' should end with a question mark.
questions.explanation: 'Are you ready' asks something, so it needs a question mark: 'Are you ready?'

questions.question: Choose the correctly punctuated question.
questions.explanation: This asks a question, so it ends with a question mark.

questions.question: Which sentence is a question?
questions.explanation: 'Did the lion roar?' asks something, making it a question.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a question mark?
options: Who wrote 'The Song of the Free'?
Who wrote 'The Song of the Free'.
Who wrote 'The Song of the Free'!
Who wrote 'The Song of the Free',
questions.explanation: 'Who wrote...' asks a question, so it must end with a question mark.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly turns 'You are coming' into a question?
questions.explanation: To make it a proper question, we reorder to 'Are you coming?' and end with a question mark.

questions.question: A question mark is placed at the very end of a question.
questions.explanation: The question mark goes at the end of the sentence that asks something.

questions.question: Which is a correctly written question?
questions.explanation: A question needs a capital letter at the start and a question mark at the end: 'Where do you live?'

questions.question: Which sentence should NOT end with a question mark?
options: The desert air resounds the calls.
questions.explanation: 'The desert air resounds the calls' is a statement, so it ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: What does an exclamation mark express?
options: Strong emotion like surprise, excitement, or urgency
questions.explanation: An exclamation mark (!) expresses strong emotion, such as surprise, excitement, anger, or urgency.

questions.question: Which sentence should end with an exclamation mark?
questions.explanation: 'Watch out' shows urgency and strong emotion, so it ends with an exclamation mark: 'Watch out!'

questions.question: We should use exclamation marks sparingly to keep their impact.
questions.explanation: The book advises using exclamation marks sparingly so they keep their strong impact.

questions.question: What symbol is an exclamation mark?
questions.explanation: An exclamation mark is written as (!).

questions.question: Which sentence best uses an exclamation mark?
questions.explanation: This shows strong excitement, so it ends with an exclamation mark.

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences that show strong emotion and could take an exclamation mark.
options: The book is on the desk
questions.explanation: 'Hurry, the bus is leaving' (urgency) and 'Wow, that's amazing' (excitement) show strong emotion. The others are calm statements.

questions.question: Which sentence uses an exclamation mark INCORRECTLY?
options: The library is open until five!
Look out, a car is coming!
questions.explanation: 'The library is open until five' is a calm statement, so it should end with a full stop, not an exclamation mark.

questions.question: An exclamation mark can show urgency, like in 'The door is closing!'
questions.explanation: An exclamation mark can show urgency and strong feeling, as in 'Watch out! The door is closing!'

questions.question: Which word or phrase most likely ends with an exclamation mark?
questions.explanation: 'Hooray' shows strong excitement, so it ends with an exclamation mark.

questions.question: Why should we not use too many exclamation marks?
options: They lose their strong effect if overused
They can only be used in questions
questions.explanation: If exclamation marks are overused, they lose their strong effect, so we use them sparingly.

questions.question: Which sentence shows the STRONGEST emotion?
questions.explanation: 'Fire! Everyone get out now!' uses exclamation marks to show strong, urgent emotion.

questions.question: The sentence 'What a beautiful day' can end with an exclamation mark to show delight.
questions.explanation: 'What a beautiful day!' uses an exclamation mark to show delight or strong feeling.

questions.question: What does a comma show in a sentence?
options: A brief pause within a sentence
questions.explanation: A comma (,) shows a brief pause within a sentence.

questions.question: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?
options: I packed a book, a pen, and my lunch.
I packed a book a pen and my lunch.
I packed. a book. a pen. and my lunch.
I packed a book? a pen? and my lunch?
questions.explanation: Commas separate items in a list: 'a book, a pen, and my lunch.'

questions.question: A comma can be used to separate items in a list.
questions.explanation: One important use of a comma is to separate items in a list, like 'apples, oranges, and bananas'.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a comma for a pause?
options: After the rain, we went outside.
After the rain we went outside.
After the rain. we went outside.
After the rain! we went outside.
questions.explanation: A comma gives a brief pause after an opening phrase: 'After the rain, we went outside.'

questions.question: Why does 'Let's eat, Grandma' mean something different from 'Let's eat Grandma'?
options: The comma shows we are talking TO Grandma, not eating her
The comma has no effect at all
The comma turns it into a question
questions.explanation: The comma changes the meaning: 'Let's eat, Grandma' invites Grandma to eat, while without the comma it sounds like we want to eat Grandma! Punctuation matters.

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences that use commas correctly.
options: We bought milk, eggs, and bread.
She is kind, helpful, and brave.
The cat, sat on the mat.
He ran, to the shop quickly.
questions.explanation: The first two use commas correctly to separate list items. The last two place commas where no pause is needed.

questions.question: Which sentence needs commas to separate a list?
options: I saw lions tigers and bears at the zoo.
I saw a lion at the zoo.
questions.explanation: 'I saw lions, tigers, and bears at the zoo.' needs commas to separate the list of animals.

questions.question: Punctuation like commas can completely change the meaning of a sentence.
questions.explanation: Yes — as shown by 'Let's eat, Grandma' versus 'Let's eat Grandma', a comma can completely change the meaning.

questions.question: What symbol is a comma?
questions.explanation: A comma is written as (,).

questions.question: Where should the comma go: 'Yes I would love to come'?
options: Yes, I would love to come.
Yes I would, love to come.
Yes I would love, to come.
Yes I would love to, come.
questions.explanation: A comma follows the opening word 'Yes' to show a brief pause: 'Yes, I would love to come.'

questions.question: Which sentence uses a comma to address someone directly?
questions.explanation: A comma is used before a name when we speak directly to someone: 'Come here, Ravi.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly lists three colours?
options: The flag is red, white, and blue.
The flag is red white and blue.
The flag is red. white. and blue.
The flag is red? white? and blue?
questions.explanation: Commas separate the colours in the list: 'red, white, and blue.'

questions.question: A comma marks the end of a complete sentence.
questions.explanation: A comma marks a brief pause WITHIN a sentence, not the end. A full stop marks the end.

questions.question: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: First, we packed our bags. Then, we left.
First we packed our bags Then we left.
First. we packed our bags. Then. we left.
First we packed our bags, Then we left,
questions.explanation: Commas follow the opening words 'First' and 'Then', and full stops end each statement.

questions.question: How many commas are needed in the list 'She bought apples oranges grapes and pears'?
questions.explanation: Three commas separate the four items: 'She bought apples, oranges, grapes, and pears.'

questions.question: A comma tells the reader to ____.
questions.explanation: A comma tells the reader to pause briefly within a sentence.

questions.question: What do quotation marks show?
options: Someone's exact spoken or written words
questions.explanation: Quotation marks (" ") are used to show someone's exact spoken or written words.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses quotation marks?
questions.explanation: Quotation marks go around the exact words spoken: She whispered, "I found it."

questions.question: Quotation marks are placed around the exact words a person says.
questions.explanation: Quotation marks surround the exact spoken or written words of a person.

questions.question: Where do the quotation marks go in: Ravi said, I am ready.
questions.explanation: The exact spoken words 'I am ready.' go inside quotation marks: Ravi said, "I am ready."

questions.question: Which sentence shows direct speech with correct punctuation?
options: The teacher said Open your books.
The teacher said, Open your books
questions.explanation: The exact words are inside quotation marks, with a comma before and a full stop inside: The teacher said, "Open your books."

questions.question: Quotation marks are also called speech marks because they show what someone said.
questions.explanation: Quotation marks are often called speech marks because they enclose the exact words someone spoke.

questions.question: Which symbol shows quotation marks?
questions.explanation: Quotation marks are written as (" ").

questions.question: Which sentence uses quotation marks INCORRECTLY?
options: "The sky is grey today." she said.
She said, "The sky is grey today."
questions.explanation: In the first option, the naming part 'she said' is wrongly placed outside with a full stop before it. It should be: "The sky is grey today," she said.

questions.question: In direct speech, what usually comes just before the opening quotation mark?
questions.explanation: A comma usually comes before the opening quotation mark, as in: She said, "Hello."

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences that correctly use quotation marks for speech.
questions.explanation: The first two use quotation marks correctly around spoken words. The last two contain no direct speech.

questions.question: Quotation marks are used when we write ____.
questions.explanation: Quotation marks are used to write the exact words someone speaks.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to write what Anu said?
options: Anu said I will help you.
Anu, said I will help you.
questions.explanation: The exact words are inside quotation marks, with a comma before and a full stop inside the marks.

questions.question: What is a contraction?
options: Two words joined and shortened, with an apostrophe for the missing letters
questions.explanation: A contraction is two words joined and shortened, using an apostrophe (') to show where letters are left out.

questions.question: What does the apostrophe show in a contraction like 'don't'?
options: Where letters have been left out
questions.explanation: In a contraction, the apostrophe shows where letters have been left out (do not → don't).

questions.question: What is the contraction of 'do not'?
questions.explanation: 'do not' becomes 'don't' — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'o'.

questions.question: What is the contraction of 'she is'?
questions.explanation: 'she is' becomes 'she's' — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'i'.

questions.question: Contractions are common in speech and informal writing.
questions.explanation: The book notes that contractions are common in speech and informal writing.

questions.question: What is the contraction of 'I am'?
questions.explanation: 'I am' becomes 'I'm' — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'a'.

questions.question: What is the contraction of 'cannot'?
questions.explanation: 'cannot' becomes 'can't' — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'no'.

questions.question: Which two words make the contraction 'they're'?
questions.explanation: 'they're' is the contraction of 'they are' — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'a'.

questions.question: Select ALL the correct contractions.
questions.explanation: 'isn't' (is not) and 'we'll' (we will) are correct. 'do'nt' and 'cant' are misspelled — they should be 'don't' and 'can't'.

questions.question: Where does the apostrophe go in the contraction of 'is not'?
questions.explanation: 'is not' becomes 'isn't' — the apostrophe goes where the 'o' was removed.

questions.question: In the poem line 'e'en time', what does the apostrophe in 'e'en' show?
options: A missing letter (it is short for 'even')
questions.explanation: 'e'en' is a poetic contraction of 'even' — the apostrophe shows the missing letter 'v'.

questions.question: The apostrophe in 'don't' takes the place of the letter 'o' from 'do not'.
questions.explanation: 'do not' becomes 'don't', and the apostrophe replaces the removed 'o'.

questions.question: What is the contraction of 'it is'?
questions.explanation: 'it is' becomes 'it's' — the apostrophe replaces the missing 'i'.

questions.question: Which sentence uses a contraction correctly?
options: I don't know if she's coming.
I do'nt know if shes coming.
I dont know if she's coming.
I don't know if shes' coming.
questions.explanation: 'don't' (do not) and 'she's' (she is) are both correctly formed contractions.

questions.question: Which two words make 'we'll'?
questions.explanation: 'we'll' is the contraction of 'we will'.

questions.question: What does an apostrophe of possession show?
questions.explanation: An apostrophe of possession (like 's) shows that something belongs to someone.

questions.question: How do we show that a bag belongs to Riya?
questions.explanation: For a singular noun, we add 's: 'Riya's bag' shows the bag belongs to Riya.

questions.question: How do we show that books belong to the students (plural ending in s)?
questions.explanation: For a plural noun already ending in 's', we add just an apostrophe: 'the students' books'.

questions.question: For a single person or thing, we add 's to show possession.
questions.explanation: For singular nouns, we add 's to show possession, like 'the dog's bone'.

questions.question: Which correctly shows that a tail belongs to one cat?
questions.explanation: For one cat (singular), we add 's: 'the cat's tail'.

questions.question: Which correctly shows a playground belonging to many children (plural not ending in s)?
questions.explanation: 'children' is plural but does not end in 's', so we add 's: 'the children's playground'.

questions.question: Select ALL the correct possessive forms.
questions.explanation: 'Riya's', 'the boys'' (plural), and 'the cat's' are correct. 'the dogs bone' is missing an apostrophe.

questions.question: Which is correct for a book belonging to James?
questions.explanation: For a singular name like James, we usually add 's: 'James's book'.

questions.question: For a plural noun that already ends in 's', we add only an apostrophe (') to show possession.
questions.explanation: For plural nouns ending in 's' (like 'students'), we add just an apostrophe after the s: 'the students' books'.

questions.question: Which sentence shows possession correctly?
options: The lion's rage echoed across the desert.
The lions rage echoed across the desert.
The lions' rage echoed, but there was one lion.
The lion rage's echoed across the desert.
questions.explanation: For one lion (singular), we add 's: 'The lion's rage'. This matches the poem's 'heart-struck lion's rage'.

questions.question: Which correctly shows a car belonging to one teacher?
questions.explanation: For one teacher (singular), we add 's: 'the teacher's car'.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'its' and 'it's'?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
questions.explanation: 'its' (no apostrophe) shows possession, while 'it's' (with apostrophe) is the contraction of 'it is'.

questions.question: The apostrophe can be used both for contractions AND to show possession.
questions.explanation: The apostrophe has two main jobs: showing missing letters in contractions, and showing possession.

questions.question: Where must we always use a capital letter?
options: At the start of every sentence
In the middle of every word
At the end of a sentence
questions.explanation: We use a capital letter at the start of every sentence.

questions.question: Which words always begin with a capital letter?
options: Names of people, places, and titles (proper nouns)
questions.explanation: Proper nouns — names of people, places, and titles — always begin with a capital letter.

questions.question: Which sentence is correctly capitalized?
questions.explanation: The sentence starts with a capital, and 'Emma', 'Paris', and 'July' are proper nouns needing capitals.

questions.question: The word 'I' is always written as a capital letter.
questions.explanation: The pronoun 'I' is always capitalised, no matter where it appears in a sentence.

questions.question: Which words in 'swami vivekananda visited chicago' need capital letters?
questions.explanation: 'Swami Vivekananda' (a person's name) and 'Chicago' (a place) are proper nouns and need capital letters.

questions.question: Which sentence uses capital letters correctly?
options: We celebrate National Youth Day in January.
we celebrate national youth day in january.
We celebrate national youth day in January.
we Celebrate National Youth Day in january.
questions.explanation: The sentence starts with a capital, and 'National Youth Day' and 'January' are proper nouns needing capitals.

questions.question: Select ALL the words that should be capitalized.
questions.explanation: 'India' (place) and 'Monday' (day) are proper nouns needing capitals. 'river' and 'table' are common nouns.

questions.question: Why does 'Emma' begin with a capital letter?
options: It is the name of a person (a proper noun)
It is at the end of a sentence
questions.explanation: 'Emma' is a person's name — a proper noun — so it begins with a capital letter.

questions.question: Which sentence has a capitalization ERROR?
questions.explanation: 'my friend lives in london.' should be 'My friend lives in London.' — the start of the sentence and 'London' both need capitals.

questions.question: The names of months and days of the week begin with capital letters.
questions.explanation: Months (January, July) and days (Monday, Sunday) are proper nouns and begin with capital letters.

questions.question: Which word needs a capital letter in 'the ramakrishna mission was founded in 1897'?
questions.explanation: 'Ramakrishna Mission' is the name of a specific organisation (a proper noun), so it needs capital letters.

questions.question: How should the title of the poem be written?
questions.explanation: In a title, the main words are capitalised: 'The Song of the Free'.

questions.question: Which is written correctly?
questions.explanation: The sentence starts with a capital, 'Anaya' (a name) is capitalised, and it ends with a full stop.

questions.question: Capital letters help show which words are important, like names and the start of sentences.
questions.explanation: Capital letters signal importance — they mark the start of sentences and proper nouns like names and places.

questions.question: Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
options: On Tuesday, Ravi visited the National Museum in Delhi.
on tuesday, ravi visited the national museum in delhi.
On tuesday, Ravi visited the national Museum in delhi.
on Tuesday, ravi Visited the National museum in Delhi.
questions.explanation: The sentence start, 'Tuesday', 'Ravi', 'National Museum', and 'Delhi' are all correctly capitalised.

questions.question: Which of these is a proper noun that must be capitalized?
questions.explanation: 'Boston' is the name of a specific place (proper noun), so it must be capitalised.

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences that are correctly capitalized.
questions.explanation: The first two correctly capitalise the sentence start and proper nouns. The last two miss capitals at the start (and 'i' should be 'I').

questions.question: The first word of every sentence should begin with a ____.
questions.explanation: The first word of every sentence begins with a capital letter.

questions.question: Which word should be capitalized in 'he passed away in 1902'?
questions.explanation: 'He' is the first word of the sentence, so it must be capitalised: 'He passed away in 1902.'

questions.question: Common nouns like 'dog', 'city', and 'book' need capital letters at the start of a sentence only if they are the first word.
questions.explanation: Common nouns are capitalised only when they begin a sentence; otherwise they stay lowercase (unlike proper nouns).

questions.question: Which is the correctly punctuated version of 'where did you put my notebook'?
options: Where did you put my notebook?
where did you put my notebook.
Where did you put my notebook.
where did you put my notebook?
questions.explanation: It needs a capital 'W' at the start and a question mark at the end: 'Where did you put my notebook?'

questions.question: Which is the correctly punctuated version of 'watch out the door is closing'?
options: Watch out! The door is closing!
watch out the door is closing
Watch out. the door is closing.
watch out? the door is closing?
questions.explanation: These show urgency, so they take exclamation marks, with capital letters at the start of each part.

questions.question: Which is the correctly punctuated version of 'she whispered i found it'?
questions.explanation: The speaker's exact words go in quotation marks, with a capital start and a full stop inside: She whispered, "I found it."

questions.question: Which is the correctly punctuated version of 'i packed a book a pen and my lunch'?
options: I packed a book, a pen, and my lunch.
i packed a book a pen and my lunch
I packed a book a pen and my lunch.
i packed a book, a pen, and my lunch
questions.explanation: It needs a capital 'I', commas to separate the list, and a full stop at the end.

questions.question: Which is the correctly punctuated version of 'i dont know if shes coming'?
options: I don't know if she's coming.
i dont know if shes coming
I dont know if shes coming.
i don't know if she's coming
questions.explanation: It needs a capital 'I', the contractions 'don't' and 'she's', and a full stop.

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences that are correctly punctuated.
options: the cat sat on the mat
questions.explanation: 'Where are you going?' and 'Watch out!' are correct. The other two lack capitals, end punctuation, and quotation marks.

questions.question: What is missing in 'Emma visited Paris last July' if it had no full stop?
options: A full stop at the end
questions.explanation: This is a complete statement, so it needs a full stop at the end.

questions.question: Which sentence has the MOST punctuation errors?
questions.explanation: 'ravi said wheres my bag' needs a capital 'R', a comma, quotation marks, an apostrophe in 'where's', and a question mark — many errors.

questions.question: Correct punctuation and capitalization make writing clearer and easier to understand.
questions.explanation: Punctuation and capital letters guide the reader, making writing clearer and easier to understand.

questions.question: Which is the correctly punctuated version of 'the teacher asked are you ready'?
options: the teacher asked are you ready
The teacher asked Are you ready.
the teacher asked, are you ready?
questions.explanation: The exact question goes inside quotation marks, with a capital start, a comma before, and a question mark inside.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly fixes 'my dogs tail is long' (one dog)?
questions.explanation: It needs a capital 'M', the possessive 'dog's' (one dog), and a full stop.

questions.question: Which end mark best completes 'What a huge wave___'?
questions.explanation: 'What a huge wave' shows strong feeling (amazement), so it best ends with an exclamation mark.

questions.question: Who wrote the poem 'The Song of the Free'?
questions.explanation: 'The Song of the Free' was written by Swami Vivekananda.

questions.question: In the first stanza, what does the wounded snake do?
questions.explanation: The poem opens: 'The wounded snake its hood unfurls' — the snake spreads its hood, suggesting a release of inner power.

questions.question: What happens to a flame when it is 'stirred up', according to the poem?
questions.explanation: 'The flame stirred up doth blaze' — when stirred, the flame blazes more strongly.

questions.question: What is the main message the poet gives to the soul in the poem?
options: March on toward your goal, for you are Divine
Give up when things get hard
Fear all the horrors of fate
questions.explanation: The poem urges: 'You are Divine. March on and on, / Nor right nor left but to the goal.' — it inspires courage and determination.

questions.question: According to the poem, when do 'Great ones unfold their best'?
options: When the soul is stirred to its inmost depth
questions.explanation: 'When the soul is stirred to its inmost depth / Great ones unfold their best.' — great people show their best when deeply challenged.

questions.question: The poem 'The Song of the Free' encourages the reader to be brave and keep moving toward their goal.
questions.explanation: The poem is inspiring — it tells the soul to march on toward its goal despite hardships, because it is Divine.

questions.question: What do the images of the wounded snake, the stirred flame, and the lightning-struck cloud have in common?
options: They all show hidden strength coming out when challenged
They all describe a peaceful garden
They all show things giving up easily
questions.explanation: Each image shows that difficulty or being 'stirred' brings out hidden strength — the poem's central idea.

questions.question: In the line 'When lightning cleaves its breast', what does the cloud do?
options: It puts forth its deluge strength
questions.explanation: 'The cloud puts forth it deluge strength / When lightning cleaves its breast' — the cloud releases its powerful downpour when struck.

questions.question: In the poem, the speaker says 'I was, I am, and I will be', suggesting the soul is eternal.
questions.explanation: The final line 'I was, I am, and I will be' suggests the soul exists across all time — it is eternal.

questions.question: What does the poet mean by 'March on and on, / Nor right nor left but to the goal'?
options: Stay focused and keep moving straight toward your goal
questions.explanation: It means to stay focused and determined — do not get distracted, but keep moving straight toward your goal.

questions.question: What kind of poem is 'The Song of the Free'?
options: An inspiring, motivational poem about inner strength
A sad poem about losing a pet
questions.explanation: It is an inspiring, motivational poem about courage, inner strength, and the divine, eternal nature of the soul.
